Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with Chinese agent being looked into by FBI, says Trump
sources.text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang should not worry about the FBI looking into his affair with a Chinese government agent.
"I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at a White House briefing.
Also read | Trump's foreign policy won't change after Republicans' midterm losses, Rubio asserts
The president called Huang, whose computer chips have helped to launch the artificial intelligence revolution, a "very honorable man." The president said he had spoken with Huang.
"I asked him about that and he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump said.
China denied on Monday it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.
Huang has acknowledged he had been intimate with a business executive, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. He did not name the woman.
Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Also read | US: Senate advances sweeping energy legislation in first major action since midterm elections
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing.
"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," Huang said in his letter.
In a routine news briefing Monday, a Chinese spokesperson rejected claims it used the woman as a spy.
"The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday.
Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China.
Nvidia shares dropped roughly 5% in pre-market trading early Monday.
The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology.
"The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.
"Those questions require evidence rather than speculation," he added in a text message to reporters.
Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning U.S. President Donald Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government.
The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.
Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations.
"Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows," the state-owned Global Times said.

sources.text:
US President Donald Trump said the FBI was looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
Mr Trump said he "was amazed" by allegations about Mr Huang, among the president's closest allies in Silicon Valley.
The US president said he had spoken to the CEO, who told him that he had no idea that the woman was a spy.
"I know the FBI is looking into it," Mr Trump said. "I think that he'll be in good shape," he added.
Nvidia shares closed down more than 4% after the company's board launched an internal investigation into whether Mr Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
The probe, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on 63-year-old Mr Huang's future, given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the CEO's role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom.
Mr Huang told Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.
Mr Huang is Nvidia's fifth-largest shareholder, with a roughly 3.6% stake, according to LSEG data, and keeps a tight grip on the company through an unusually flat structure in which dozens of executives report directly to him.
However, unlike Mark Zuckerberg's Meta Platforms or Elon Musk's SpaceX, Nvidia has no dual-class shares that would give co-founder Mr Huang majority voting control.
The New York Times reported that Mr Trump was briefed on Mr Huang's relationship with the woman and that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and that the president chose not to act on the information.
"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
Mr Huang's relationship with Mr Trump has coincided with several favorable policy developments for the company, and the president has lavished Mr Huang with praise, awarding him the nation's highest honor for scientific achievement in October.
The same day Mr Trump gave Mr Huang the award, the president disclosed buying up to $1.6 million and selling up to $1 million of Nvidia shares during the summer.
'Not an ordinary CEO'
Nvidia said its board has confidence in Mr Huang, thought by many on Wall Street to be the most important person underpinning the AI trade.
Analysts acknowledged uncertainty around succession, but most do not expect the investigation to result in the longtime CEO stepping down.
"Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he is Nvidia, clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and pulls most of the company's strings himself," said Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein.
Nvidia shareholders were quick to sue Mr Huang and the company in a proposed class action yesterday, accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Mr Huang's ties with a suspected Chinese spy.
Politicians and advocates told Reuters that Congress was more likely to pass legislation to tighten China's access to AI chips in light of news of Mr Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent.
US House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said that Congress needs more answers and called for the House to pass an annual defence bill that includes restrictions on chip sales to China.

President Donald Trump has said that the FBI was looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang a day after the tech executive admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.
“We’ll look into it,” Trump told reporters on Nov. 9. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape.”
Trump said he spoke with Huang on Nov. 9 and asked him about the situation.
“He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” Trump said. “I asked him that question. ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him.
“I hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we'll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem.”
Shares of Nvidia tumbled at the start of the trading week as Wall Street waits for the outcome of the investigation and its potential implications for Nvidia’s leadership.
Alice Huang and Megaspeed
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed.
The New York Times first reported on the Nvidia CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang and U.S. intelligence agencies’ concerns that she passed information to Beijing.
President Donald Trump had been briefed on the intelligence last year.
Megaspeed has purchased Nvidia chips, and U.S. authorities have investigated allegations that the company helped China gain access to advanced AI processors subject to U.S. export restrictions.
The probe comes amid a broader “Singapore washing” trend, in which some Chinese companies establish or domicile businesses in Singapore to reduce exposure to U.S.–China tensions and preserve access to global markets and technology.
The practice has spread across multiple industries, including technology, biotechnology, and critical minerals.
It is unclear what information Alice Huang may have shared with China.
“The central questions are whether intellectual property or sensitive information was compromised, whether customer relationships or export approvals are affected, and whether there is a material change in leadership,” Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management, told The Epoch Times in an email.
Allegedly Targeted by Chinese Spy Effort
Nvidia’s board stated that it will form a committee of independent directors, with help from external independent counsel, to oversee an investigation.
Although Huang may have been the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the board stated that it has no reason to think that national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.
Huang supports the review and has committed to cooperating with the probe, the company stated.
“The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” Nvidia said.
Export Controls
The White House implemented strict export controls on the company’s most advanced AI chips to Beijing, forcing Nvidia to produce China-specific chips to comply with U.S. regulations.
Chinese AI companies have increasingly turned to domestic alternatives, including chips developed by Huawei and other local firms.
Huang has been highly critical of U.S. export controls, calling them a “failure.”
“Four years ago, Nvidia had 95 percent market share in China. Today, it is only 50 percent,” Huang said at a news conference at last year’s Computex technology show in Taipei, Taiwan.
“The rest is Chinese technology. They have a lot of local technology they would use if they didn’t have Nvidia.”
Chinese AI firms have adapted by using locally developed chips, with export restrictions and state support bolstering domestic competitors.
Lawmakers’ Response
Lawmakers have requested a closed-door briefing regarding Nvidia’s security protocols and Huang’s interactions with the former Megaspeed executive.
In a Nov. 4 letter, three committees, including the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, asked Huang to appear in Washington.
“We are writing to request that you appear before our committees for a joint, closed-door briefing on Nvidia’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset,” the letter reads.
Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) told The Epoch Times on Nov. 9 that he had not been briefed on the situation yet but that he thought Huang should come before the Senate Intelligence Committee, and he said he planned to speak with his colleagues on the committee about that.
“We need to get to the bottom of what was exchanged with this Chinese intelligence agent,” Kelly said.
Sen. Christopher Coons (D-Del.) told The Epoch Times that to see the CEO of “one of the most important, cutting-edge AI companies clearly in a relationship” with an alleged Chinese agent raises significant national security risks.
He questioned how much that might have influenced the Nvidia CEO’s effort to export cutting-edge chips to China and if any critical U.S. policy toward China might have been compromised.
The senators said they believe that more than one senate committee will want to look into the issue.
“Congress has a real oversight role, and we should look very hard,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) told The Epoch Times.
How Wall Street Reacted
Nvidia shares slipped in after-hours trading on Nov. 8 after Huang admitted to the infidelity and the board announced an independent investigation.
The stock fell by 4.27 percent to $178.67 at the end of the Nov. 9 trading session.
Despite the scandal surrounding Huang, many analysts do not anticipate that it will sink the stock long-term. However, the main threat is whether the company will force Jensen Huang out after 33 years.
“You would not want to see Jensen removed as CEO; we think that the stock would be in even tougher shape than it is now if that were to happen,” Mahoney said.
“His technical vision, execution, industry relationships, and ability to articulate the AI opportunity have been major competitive advantages.”
At the same time, Mahoney said, Nvidia also benefits from engineering talent, a well-established software ecosystem, and strong customer demand.
Chinese Honeypot Operations
Over the years, U.S. adversaries, including China, have been accused of employing so-called honeypot tactics as part of intelligence and influence operations.
The strategy involves using romantic or personal relationships to gather information, gain access to influential networks, or exert leverage over targets in government, business, and academia.
Swalwell never publicly admitted to the relationship. He resigned in April after sexual allegations involving a former staffer surfaced.

Nvidia spy allegations likely to spur laws to tighten China’s access to AI chips, say some lawmakers
NEW YORK - The US Congress is more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China’s access to AI chips in light of news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent, lawmakers and advocates said.
Three chip-related measures are slated for possible inclusion in the annual defence authorisation bill for fiscal year 2027, which began in October. 
Huang’s affair, and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump, has added new urgency to concerns about China’s access to advanced chips that could undermine US national security.
The measures are the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over advanced chip exports, the Chip Security Act, which would require businesses to track their chips to combat smuggling, and the Match Act, which would push US allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment to China.
Nvidia is considered the biggest opponent of both the Chip Security and AI Overwatch acts, according to one former congressional staff member who had direct contact with the company over several months.
Until the US Department of Justice brought indictments tied to chip smuggling last year, Huang and Nvidia had argued there was no such smuggling. The company said it complied with export laws.
Nvidia declined to comment.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all three bills earlier this year. They are now in the Senate National Defense Authorization Act management package.
In a joint statement on Nov 9, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and her Republican colleague Jim Banks of Indiana said that “Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent”.
They added: “It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips.”
In March, the senators had urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia’s export licences to China and conduct a full security review.
Democratic Representative Bill Foster of Illinois echoed the senators’ sentiments. “Congress has the tools to prevent powerful AI chips from getting in the wrong hands and posing a national security risk,” Foster posted on X on Nov 10, in response to news of Huang’s affair.
He said the Chip Security Act he introduced with Republican Representative Bill Huizenga of Michigan had passed unanimously out of committee in the House. “It’s time to get it across the finish line,” he said.
“The hurdle these bills need to clear is getting the White House onboard,” said Chris MacKenzie, a spokesman for Americans for Responsible Innovation, a Washington non-profit organisation that favours the measures. “With everything that’s surfaced, it would be costly for the White House to back Nvidia in a fight with Congress over restricting Chinese access to chips.”
The White House did not comment on the measures.

The Spy Who Loved Jensen Huang: Everything We Know So Far
sources.text:
Artificial-intelligence giant Nvidia announced on Sunday that it has opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to the board that he’d had an affair with a business executive whom the U.S. government believes is a spy for China. In a companywide letter, Huang told employees: “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He also said he supports the investigation “and will cooperate fully” and that “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”
Given Nvidia’s dominance in the AI industry, its clout on Wall Street, Huang’s ties to Donald Trump, and the whole suspected Chinese spy at the center of it all, this is obviously not your typical workplace affair.
So what has the president said about all this? Have Democratic congressional leaders, what with their newfound power come January, weighed in? How has the stock market reacted? Has Huang’s family spoken out? Here’s what we know so far.
  
  
    .
Who is Jensen Huang?
    
Huang is the Taiwan-born co-founder of Nvidia, which he started in 1993 with two friends. (They came up with the idea for the company at a Silicon Valley Denny’s.) Today Huang is one of the most powerful industry players, having “transformed Nvidia from a maker of video-game graphics chips into the world’s dominant supplier of AI processors.” Nvidia has a market capitalization of roughly $4.5 trillion. Huang himself was worth approximately $150 billion prior to the Sunday revelation; he lost a few billion to his name after the affair went public. He’s known for wearing black leather jackets, which have been purchased as collector’s items.
  
  
    .
Who is Alice Huang?
    
Alice Huang (or Huang Le) is a business executive whom U.S. intelligence began electronically surveilling more than a year ago. “Information on Ms. Huang’s background is largely absent from the Chinese internet,” according to the New York Times, which noted that an online biography said “she worked in China as a TV reporter before becoming a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company that had become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia,” buying “more than $4.8 billion in chips since June 2024.”
That company, Megaspeed, has been under investigation by the Commerce Department since last year “for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China.” The Times reported that “as Megaspeed’s chip purchases rolled in, Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang” — who are unrelated — “began spending time together.”
In June 2024, he joined her at a bar in Taipei after a local technology trade show. They drank whiskey alongside other A.I. executives. A year later, they dined at a restaurant in Taipei with other executives. Taiwanese media captured her giving him a kiss on the cheek and standing behind him as he spoke to journalists.
Officials in Washington were said to be intensely worried about the relationship, especially given that they were “already alarmed by the large volume of Megaspeed’s purchases.”
  
  
    .
Who is Huang apologizing to in his companywide letter?
    
The Nvidia CEO has been married to Lori Huang since 1985. They met at Oregon State University, where he has said he got into her lab group and attempted to impress her with his brain. “I walked up to her and said, ‘Do you want to see my homework?’” he recalled in 2024. “Then I made her a promise: ‘If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you, you’ll get straight A’s.’”
On the podcast How I Built This, Juang said that while he was building Nvidia, “Lori took care of everything and I don’t remember her complaining one time. That’s the gift that she gave me.” (It is not clear if the couple have a prenup. California, where they live, is a community-property state that dictates all assets and debts acquired during the marriage are divided equally in a divorce.)
The Huangs have two children, Madison and Spencer, who work for Nvidia, as does their son-in-law.
  
  
    .
Did the Nvidia CEO say anything publicly about the relationship before Sunday?
    
Indeed he did, telling Bloomberg News last month that any interactions he had with Ms. Huang had been “related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.”
  
  
    .
Did anyone in Washington sound any really loud alarms about the affair?
    
As it happens, Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly “oversaw the drafting of the highly classified memo this past spring warning top Trump administration officials that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.” That memo, per the Times, was written after U.S. officials determined Ms. Huang “had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security.”
The memo was reportedly sent to officials with high-level security clearances prior to a trip the president took to China in May, and it may or may not have played a role in Jensen Huang not initially being invited to join Trump, per the Times.
Huang was initially left off the list of major business and tech executives invited to join Mr. Trump in China. It is unclear whether the exclusion was connected to the memo. By that point, a number of people inside the administration were concerned about Mr. Huang’s influence on the president’s policy of only lightly regulating A.I., people briefed on the matter said.
After Mr. Trump saw media coverage about Mr. Huang being absent from the delegation, the president asked him to join the trip by meeting Air Force One during a layover in Alaska. The president drafted a social media post saying that it was an honor to have “the Great Jensen Huang,” and other business leaders “journeying to the Great Country of China where I will be asking President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction, to ‘open up’ China so that these brilliant people can work their magic.”
  
  
    .
What has China said?
    
“The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday.
  
  
    .
Has Trump weighed in?
    
He sure has, in his typical way, telling reporters, of Huang, “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong” and that “he dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.” (Did the president mean “everybody” has affairs with suspected Chinese spies? That “everybody” has affairs generally? Unclear.) The president also said he believes the Nvidia CEO is “an honorable guy” and “probably has an excuse for it.” He added that he did not regret not acting on earlier intelligence.
  
  
    .
Has Congress responded?
    
Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely become House majority leader in January, told CBS News on Monday that the matter is “a significant issue of concern.” He said there is a classified briefing being held at the White House today, where he expects the affair will be a topic of conversation. On Saturday, Democratic senator Chris Coons, who is expected to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote on X that “Congress will investigate and get answers.”
Representative Michael McCaul, a Texas Republican who serves as vice-chair of the House Committee on Homeland Security, wrote on X on Saturday: “The U.S. should immediately pause the shipment of advanced AI chips to China until we can get to the bottom of this incident and ensure our national security is not being undermined.”
Huang has resisted calls for stronger government regulation on the export of advanced AI chips.
  
  
    .
Has Elon Musk offered his two cents?
    
You know he has.
  
  
    .
Who is running the investigation?
    
The company said on Sunday the board will choose an outside counsel to probe the affair and that Huang will not be part of selecting who that counsel will be. Also worth noting, per the Times: “At Nvidia, Huang is the sole public face of the company and has no clear second-in-command. He decides which projects are a strategic priority, and frequently sends short emails to individual engineers about details. Huang has said he has 60 direct reports and reviews every employee’s salary.”
Any suggestion that Huang will be replaced at the company is “comedy,” Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC on Monday.

In remarks to staff, Mr Huang told Nvidia employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, though he did not provide details about the relationship.
Mr Huang is Nvidia’s fifth-largest shareholder, holding a roughly 3.6% stake, according to LSEG data. He also maintains tight control through an unusually flat management structure in which dozens of executives report directly to him.
Still, Nvidia’s governance differs from other tech titans such as Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta Platforms or Elon Musk’s SpaceX: the chipmaker does not have dual-class shares that would grant co-founder Mr Huang majority voting control.
The New York Times reported that Mr Trump was briefed on Mr Huang’s relationship with the woman, including allegations that she was providing information to the Chinese government, and that the president chose not to act on the information.
In Beijing, China’s Foreign Ministry rejected the claims. “The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters.
Mr Huang’s ties with Mr Trump have coincided with several policy developments that have benefited Nvidia. The president has also publicly praised Mr Huang, awarding him the nation’s highest honor for scientific achievement in October.
On the same day he presented the award, Mr Trump disclosed that he had bought up to $1.6 million and sold up to $1 million of Nvidia shares during the summer.
‘Not an ordinary CEO’
Nvidia said its board remains confident in Mr Huang, who many on Wall Street view as the central figure supporting the AI trade.
While analysts pointed to uncertainty over succession, most said they do not expect the investigation to end with the longtime CEO stepping down.
Nvidia shares closed down more than 4% after the company’s board launched an internal investigation
“Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he is Nvidia, clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and pulls most of the company’s strings himself,” said Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein.
Nvidia shareholders moved quickly to sue Mr Huang and the company in a proposed class action yesterday, alleging they defrauded investors by concealing Mr Huang’s ties with a suspected Chinese spy.
Politicians and advocates told Reuters that the revelations about Mr Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent could make Congress more likely to pass legislation aimed at tightening China’s access to AI chips.
US House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Congress needs more answers and urged the House to pass an annual defence bill that includes restrictions on chip sales to China.

Trump stands by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang despite spy scandal, but FBI is investigating
The revelations this weekend that Nvidia Corp. boss Jensen Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman who has been accused of working for Chinese intelligence have now ensnared U.S. President Donald Trump, raising further questions about national security.
At the same time, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said it’s looking into the affair, meaning it’s likely to get continuing attention in coming weeks or longer.
Nvidia said it has launched an investigation into Chief Executive Huang’s actions after he admitted to cheating on his wife with a woman known as Alice Huang (no relation), who serves as the CEO of a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.
U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang has been feeding information about Huang and the chipmaker’s plans to the Chinese government. And though Trump was informed of the possible infiltration, he has continued working with Nvidia and Huang on domestic policy issues related to technology and artificial intelligence, which have become of vital importance to the U.S. economy.
Huang has spent the last two years cultivating a close relationship with Trump, gaining extraordinary access to America’s top decision-maker and influence over the country’s AI strategy. He has gone from being virtually unknown to the president to being a key member of a cadre of technology industry executives accompanying him on trips aboard Air Force One, including a visit to China in May.
He has come to be seen as a major ally of Trump, attending numerous White House events while repeatedly praising his policies. Notably, his company made a $25 million donation to the president’s gaudy ballroom project, becoming its top corporate contributor alongside Apple Inc.
Those efforts seem to have gone a long way toward getting Huang into the president’s good graces, and it seems to have paid off for the company. Last year, after months of lobbying from Huang and Nvidia, the Trump administration agreed that it could sell more advanced chips to China that were previously banned from being exported to the country.
Though that decision was widely known, it seems that the Trump administration has intervened in other ways to protect Nvidia’s interests. Earlier today, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling banned chips into China, was abruptly canceled after receiving an email from Nvidia’s general counsel. Commerce official Jeff Kessler, who was nominated for the role by Trump, reportedly gave Nvidia permission to contact the investigation team and mention his name, which goes against standard protocol.
Investigators had grown suspicious that Megaspeed was essentially just a front for smuggling embargoed Nvidia chips into China, but the correspondence from Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter kicked off a kerfuffle that ultimately led to the investigation being transferred to the Department of Justice.
But Trump defended Huang late on Sunday, stating that the Nvidia boss is an “honorable guy” who has not committed any wrongdoing. The president had been briefed about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation as far back as October 2025, but decided not to do anything, according to the Times. “I haven’t heard that he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody, but, you know, so does everybody else.”
Trump continued to defend Huang on Monday when quizzed about the situation again, before revealing that the Federal Bureau of Investigation is also looking into his relationship with the suspected spy. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” he said at a White House briefing.
Despite the apparent protection afforded by Trump, Huang appears to be taking no chances. A report in Wired said today that the Nvidia boss has hired the services of a public relations firm called Heller that specializes in handling public scandals. Rise Heller, the firm’s founder, has developed a reputation for helping powerful men sidestep allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies. She previously represented clients including the former Congressman Anthony Weiner, the writer Jeffrey Toobin and the chef Mario Batali, Wired reported.
Tech industry personalities have also leapt to Huang’s defense. Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital said in a post on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” and stressed that although he did something “incredibly dumb,” he believes there was “no bad intention.” Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk later shared Maguire’s post, saying he agrees with all of it.
However, no intervention has managed to protect Nvidia’s stock, which slid more than 4% on Monday, wiping around $190 billion off of the company’s valuation.
Nvidia is scheduled to hold its next financial earnings call on Nov. 17, in which Huang is likely to face some very difficult questions — if he is on the call as has been customary.
